There is an hour before dawn that belongs to no one. The streetlights are still on, but they've begun to look embarrassed, casting their yellow pools onto pavement that doesn't need them anymore. Birds haven't quite committed to the day. The world holds its breath.

I love this hour because it's honest. Nothing is performing yet. The day's façade hasn't been assembled—no traffic, no errands, no carefully composed versions of ourselves heading out to meet the world. There's just the raw material of a day, unformed, still soft enough to be anything.

I wonder how many decisions have been made in this hour, quietly, by people sitting at kitchen tables with their hands around warm mugs. How many letters written and not sent. How many resolutions formed and abandoned by breakfast. The pre-dawn is where we rehearse our lives, saying the words we can't quite say in daylight.

And then the sun comes up, and the hour closes like water closing over a stone, and all those private truths get tucked away while we put on our public faces and step out into the ordinary business of being people.

But the hour keeps its secrets. It will come again tomorrow, patient and dim, waiting to collect the next batch of unspoken things. And somewhere, someone will be awake to meet it—a nurse coming off shift, a baker turning on the ovens, a stranger staring at the ceiling, rehearsing a sentence they may never find the courage to say.
